rows.en: But the days of tranquillity did not last long. Yannai returned from his wars, and for an unknown reason his heart turned against the Pharisees. Then it happened once, on the Festival of Tabernacles, that he stood on the altar to pour out the water on the festival according to the custom of the Pharisees. But with special intent he did not do it as commanded; rather he poured the water on his feet, to show the Pharisees that he did not acknowledge the water libation (Sukkah 48b). This was a clear sign to them that his heart was not loyal to the Pharisees, and from his deeds they recognized his intention, that he was seeking a pretext to come against the Pharisees with a charge. Because of this, wrath broke out on the part of the people, and they pelted him with their etrogim and called him "son of a captive woman" (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 13). Then he rose against them in burning anger and took his revenge, and made a great slaughter among them. There was then a fierce strife between him and the people, and his hatred of the Pharisees grew day by day. He hanged eight hundred of the rebels on the tree, and of those who followed the Pharisees some fled (Megillat Ta'anit ch. 12) and some hid, and matters were not restored until after his death. Simeon too was in hiding from the king's wrath. But it is not known for certain whether he was among the rebels and escaped with his life like all his companions, or whether the cause of his flight was another quarrel that arose between him and Yannai. For it is told thus: Once three hundred poor Nazirites came, and Simeon interceded for them before Yannai, that he should give from his money enough for half the offerings that they were obliged to bring for their naziriteship, and he (Simeon) himself would undertake to give them the remaining half. Yannai granted his request and gave half the offerings, and Simeon used a stratagem and released the vow of half of them, so that they no longer needed an offering. The matter became known to Yannai, and his wrath against Simeon was great, because he had dared to make sport of him; and for this reason Simeon hid from him. So the cause of his flight is told. And of the cause of his return it is told: At that time noble princes came from Persia to visit Yannai in his palace. As they sat at the banquet, they said to Yannai: We remember that many years ago, when we were here to visit you in your palace as today, an old man sat before you all of whose words were wisdom, and we delighted in them; why has he not come to the banquet today as at other times? Then, at his guests' request, Yannai sent messengers to seek Simeon, to call him and to assure him that he had forgotten how he had provoked the eyes of his glory and that he wished to make peace with him. He was sought and found, and Simeon did as the king said and came before him. Yannai bade him sit, and Simeon set his seat between the king and the queen. But Yannai, although he had promised Simeon to make peace with him, still could not restrain himself from demanding an account from Simeon of the affair with the Nazirites, and he asked him: Now tell me, what led your heart to make sport of me? Simeon answered and said: I did not make sport of you; I spoke what is right and true. For just as you gave half the offerings from your money, so I exempted them from the second half by my Torah; and do you not know that "wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence" [Ecclesiastes 7:12]? "And why did you hide by fleeing?" He answered him: Because of your anger, for I said to myself, "hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast" [Isaiah 26:20]! Yannai went on and asked him: Why did you set your seat between the king and the queen? Simeon answered him: So it befits masters of wisdom, according to the words of Ben Sira: "Exalt her, and she shall promote thee, and she will seat you among princes."⚠1 Then Yannai ordered that Simeon be given a cup of wine to say the Grace after Meals. They gave him the cup, and Simeon began: Let us bless for the food that Yannai and his companions have eaten. Yannai said to him: Indeed you are still in your stubbornness. "But," said Simeon, "shall I say: Let us bless for the food that I have not eaten?" Then Yannai ordered that he be given food, and he ate and said the blessing as is proper (Yerushalmi Berakhot 7:2 and Nazir 5:5; Genesis Rabbah 91; and Ecclesiastes Rabbah). So the cause of his flight and of his return is told. But be it one way or the other, in any case we see that there was a great rift between him and the sages, so much so that even Simeon, who was (according to some) the queen's brother, feared that for so small a cause he would kill him. Indeed there is no doubt that Simeon's return was for the good and benefit of all the Pharisees: even if matters were not restored to their former strength, Yannai still did not persecute them, through Simeon's efforts. Indeed, after Yannai's death the Pharisees returned to their place in the Sanhedrin; and Yannai himself recognized at the end of his days that if the Jewish ruler leaned on the Pharisees, his kingdom would be firm in his hand, since most of the people followed them and conducted themselves by their counsel. Accordingly he advised his wife Shelaminon [Salome Alexandra] before his death to strengthen the hands of the Pharisees (*Antiquities*, ibid.). And these were the last words he spoke to his wife: Fear neither the Pharisees nor those who are not Pharisees; fear the hypocrites who resemble Pharisees, who do the deed of Zimri and seek the reward of Phinehas (Sotah 22b).

1.note: The first half is Proverbs 4:8; the second half is Ben Sira 11:1. Weiss gives the whole as Ben Sira, as the sources do.

rows.en: Shelaminon kept Yannai's last words, because they agreed with the desire of her heart; for she had long favoured the ways of the Pharisees. Immediately after her husband's death she made a covenant with the Pharisees, and her desire prospered in her hand, for the Pharisees upheld her rule. Then Simeon stood with all his strength against the Sadducees. His first effort was to make a public demonstration against them, and all the teachings he taught and the ordinances he enacted were aimed against the views of the Sadducees, to uproot them. The sages of that time gave a general reinforcement to their words by expounding from the book of the Torah of Moses that any man who rebels against a statute of the Torah and rules on that statute in a way other than the statute was understood according to the views of the majority of a Sanhedrin of Pharisees, his ruling being for practice, is called a rebellious elder (zaken mamre), and his sentence is death; for he is the man of whom, according to the midrash of the Pharisees, it is said: "even that man shall die: and thou shalt put away the evil from Israel" (Deuteronomy 17:12). Whether this statute was decreed for every kind of ruling that touches any one of the commandments of the Lord, or was said only of matters whose wilful transgression incurs karet, as one of the sages of the Mishnah holds, this we cannot decide. But an old halakhah, cited as an example to show in what way the rebellious elder becomes liable, is the witness and the proof that the point was not the severity of the punishment; rather, everything depended on whether the elder's ruling opposed one of the words of the Scribes in the interpretation of the Torah. For that halakhah gives as an example: one who says there are five totafot (in tefillin), to add to the words of the Scribes, is liable.{v1_08_04:1} Indeed, in the days of the later sages the original reason of the statute had already been lost, and it no longer had any practical purpose, only a theoretical one. Therefore it came to be counted among several other laws that were no longer practised, which they studied only to "magnify the Torah and make it glorious" [Isaiah 42:21]; and at times they drew consequences from it by the ways of their midrash which had not been so in former times, while the statute was still alive in practice. And perhaps already at that time they gave reinforcement also to the ordinances and decrees of the Scribes, and based them on the word of the Torah, "thou shalt not decline from the sentence which they shall shew thee" [Deuteronomy 17:11], meaning: the Torah obliges one to act according to the teaching of the Scribes even where they do not come by the force of their midrash.{v1_08_04:2} This, then, is the general reinforcement; but in particular matters too there is opposition with a special intent. Most of the halakhot mentioned in the name of Simeon ben Shetaḥ are laws in matters of judicial statutes, in capital and monetary cases. Opposition in this area was most necessary for them, since during the whole time that the hand of the Sadducees was uppermost they enacted statutes that were not in accordance with the Torah in the view of the Pharisees, and they dared to make a book of statutes on capital and monetary law. Some of those statutes have come down to us. The Sadducees used to say: A plotting witness (ed zomem) is not put to death until the accused has been put to death (Makkot 5b). Judah ben Tabbai himself relates that he put a plotting witness to death for his intent, to remove [the view] from the hearts of the Sadducees, who used to say that plotting witnesses are not put to death until [the accused] has been put to death. In his zeal he overstepped the bounds and erred in law, putting to death the one witness proven a plotter when the second witness had not been proven a plotter; and Simeon ben Shetaḥ rebuked him, saying: You have shed innocent blood, for the sages said: Plotting witnesses are not put to death until both of them are proven plotters (ibid., and Ḥagigah 16b; Tosefta Sanhedrin ch. 6; and Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 20). But this was agreed among them: that plotting witnesses are put to death for their intent if the verdict against the accused has been concluded; and that is the meaning of the halakhah: "a plotting witness is not put to death until the verdict has been concluded." The statute that plotting witnesses are put to death only if the accused was put to death on their testimony was newly enacted by the Sadducees, but the Pharisees' understanding of the law of hazamah was the received one; for from of old it was a statute that plotting witnesses were judged with the fitting punishment even for their intent. Indeed there is no doubt that when they said, "a plotting witness is not put to death until the verdict has been concluded," they did not mean to exclude the case where they killed, as if they are then not put to death; for if we say so, the measure of justice would be defective. And although the later sages thought so, and one whose personal name is not known said, "If they did not kill, they are put to death; if they killed, they are not put to death" (Makkot 5b), he did not say this from tradition; it is his own opinion. For had this been a tradition received by all the sages, the father of that sage would not have contradicted his son from reasoning and the judgment of the intellect (also there). But this stood firm: plotting witnesses are judged for their intent. Already in the days of the author of the apocryphal story "Susanna" the law of hazamah was understood in this way. For he relates that the two elders who testified against Susanna that she had committed harlotry were proven plotters after her death sentence had been concluded, and they were dealt with according to the law of Moses: "then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother" [Deuteronomy 19:19] (Susanna 61, 62). The time of composition of this story is very early, for in it the law of hazamah was still understood in a way far removed from its meaning in the days of Simeon ben Shetaḥ. For according to that story the witnesses contradicted one another in the examination: one said that Susanna had committed the lewd act under an oak, and the other said under a terebinth;⚠1 and because of this contradiction they judged that they had testified falsely against her, and sentenced them to death according to the law of plotting witnesses. And it is true that several traces of this understanding are found in the books of the Oral Torah, which have preserved for us old halakhot in this area whose plain sense upholds this understanding. When they said, "he is not liable until he contradicts himself," "until they prove themselves plotters," "the witness makes himself false, makes his fellow false" (Sifre Shofetim §§189, 190), do these expressions not show that the essence of hazamah is the contradiction of the witnesses, so that through the contradiction, when they contradict one another in the inquiries or contradict themselves, it becomes clear that they testified falsely? And this understanding agrees with the understanding of the law in the days of the writer of the story of Susanna. But at a later time they gave all these expressions another sense, and explained them all as hazamah that comes from outside, through other witnesses who testify about the persons of the first witnesses (Geiger, *Urschrift*, p. 196).⚠2 But this seems clear: the halakhah that Simeon put forward in the name of his predecessors, "plotting witnesses are not put to death until both are proven plotters," can be explained only if we decide that the hazamah comes from outside; for of witnesses who contradict one another one cannot say that both were proven plotters. Certainly this halakhah speaks of hazamah that comes from other witnesses; and already in Simeon's days they had changed the reason of the old halakhah.

1.he: תחת אלון והשני אמר תחת אלה
1.note: Weiss's Hebrew tree names; in the Greek Susanna (54, 58) the trees are a mastic and a holm oak.

2.note: Read as R. Abraham Geiger, Urschrift (Breslau 1857), p. 196.

rows.en: Indeed, this ancient halakhah, that plotting witnesses are judged for their intent, which the Sadducees removed from their statute of law and which Simeon ben Shetaḥ and Judah ben Tabbai restored, had great consequences. The first: that witnesses who have testified, and the verdict has been concluded on their word, cannot retract and testify otherwise. For if witnesses could retract and testify otherwise, how could it happen that plotting witnesses are put to death once the verdict has been concluded? Could they not retract their first words? And we have a clear hint, in a story of an incident that happened in those days, that this halakhah concerning the retraction of witnesses from their words is closely related to the ancient halakhah mentioned above; and if we look into the matter we see that the one is a consequence of the other. For it is told that Simeon ben Shetaḥ sentenced eighty women sorcerers and hanged them on the tree in one day (Sanhedrin 45b). This was evil in the eyes of their relatives, and they wished to take revenge on him. Two base men arose and testified against Simeon's son that he had committed a capital sin. And as he was led out to be executed, the witnesses repented and confessed that they had testified falsely. And the condemned man said to his father: Father, if you seek to bring deliverance through your hand, make me as a threshold (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin ch. 6). From this one may judge that Simeon wished to believe the witnesses who had retracted their testimony. But the son reminded his father that the teaching of the Pharisees in the laws of testimony does not allow witnesses to retract their first testimony after the verdict has been concluded. For if witnesses could retract and testify otherwise, it would be impossible to punish plotting witnesses for their intent and put them to death even if they did not kill: would not every witness, if proven a plotter, retract his testimony and go free? And this halakhah, "if they did not kill, they are put to death," was surely among the greatest points of opposition between the Sadducees and the Pharisees. Whether the Sadducees also opposed the halakhah that witnesses are not put to death until both are proven plotters is not known to us; but it seems that, although Simeon brought it from his predecessors, it was not widely known, for we see that Judah ben Tabbai erred in it and thought that even if only one witness was proven a plotter he is put to death (Makkot 5b, and in several places). No doubt Judah's error came to him from the sense of the verse that says, "and, behold, if the witness be a false witness" [Deuteronomy 19:18], which, taken literally, refers also to a single witness. But Simeon ben Shetaḥ relied on a binyan av: in one place the Torah was precise and wrote "one witness" [Deuteronomy 19:15], to teach that wherever "witness" is said without qualification it is to be understood in a general sense and refers to complete testimony, that is, two witnesses (Sotah 2b). Now there is no doubt that the Sadducees too expounded the words literally, as was their way, and put a plotting witness to death even if both were not plotters.{v1_08_06:1} Several halakhot we learn from an incident that happened to him with King Yannai. Yannai's slave killed a person. They sent word to Yannai: Your slave has killed a person. Yannai sent his slave to the court. But they answered him that he himself was obliged to come, since by the law of the Torah the master stands trial for the damages of his slave, just as the owner of an ox must stand trial for his ox. Yannai came and sat before them. Simeon ben Shetaḥ said to him: King Yannai, stand on your feet and give honour to the statute of the Torah, as it is said: "Then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand" [Deuteronomy 19:17]. Yannai said to him: Not as you say, but as your colleagues say. But his colleagues, out of fear of the king, were silent. Simeon said to them: You are men of [hidden] thoughts; let the Master of thoughts come and exact punishment from you (Sanhedrin 19a). Now if on the one side we see that Simeon showed no favour in judgment, on the other side it appears that Simeon himself recognized from this incident that not every time is fit to hold fast to the rule "let the law pierce the mountain"; for because of this incident it became a statute: The king does not judge and is not judged (Sanhedrin 19b). From the details of this incident we also learn two further principles in the understanding of the laws of the Torah. The first: that the slave was regarded by them as a man's ox. The second: that they understood the verse "Then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand" literally: not as referring to coming forward to judgment, but that the word "shall stand" is to be understood as actual standing, teaching that the litigant is obliged to stand (Shevu'ot 30a).{v1_08_06:2}

The strife with the Sadducees and the victory over them brought to light several laws in various matters. In that time is found the first trace of the midrash on the statute of the Torah "eye for eye" [Exodus 21:24], whose meaning is payment for an eye (Bava Kamma 83a; Mekhilta Mishpatim), against the view of the Sadducees, who said: an actual eye. The Sadducees' view in this is the view found among all the ancient lawgivers of most lands{v1_08_06:3}⚠3; and the first among the nations who had the statute of paying for bodily injuries with money were the Romans. Now it is an error to think that the Pharisees shaped this statute of the Torah according to what they knew of the law of retaliation among the Romans. For this description is rooted in the nature of man's recognition of law and justice; and since this recognition of justice changes according to the level of enlightenment, the law of retaliation laid down in this statute also changes, and becomes different among a people that has risen from step to step on the ladder of enlightenment from what it was among that same people while it stood on a lower step of that ladder. Therefore the change in the recognition of justice, and the product of that recognition, which is the change in the meaning of the statute, are natural matters and are alike among every people. Now this interpretation of the statute "eye for eye" as referring to payment of money they did not take from any nation; it was original among the Jews, and they weighed, searched out and founded it from their inner recognition of justice and according to the level of enlightenment to which they rose in the course of time. Likewise the interpretations that the Sadducees gave of the statute of one who brings an evil name upon his wife, saying that the meaning of the Torah's words "and they shall spread the cloth" [Deuteronomy 22:17] is literal, and likewise that the words "and spit in his face" in the statute of ḥalitzah [Deuteronomy 25:9] mean only the literal sense, that she should spit in his very face, that is, on the surface of the face: all these were abolished in the days of Simeon ben Shetaḥ (Megillat Ta'anit ch. 4).{v1_08_07:1} On one matter Simeon and his colleagues strove with the Sadducees with great force, and the strife lasted eight days, until they defeated the Sadducees. For the Sadducees said that the daily offering (tamid) comes from the property of an individual, and they did not want the daily offerings to be offered from public funds, since this caused great expense to the Temple treasury. Their proof was from the Torah's words, "The one lamb shalt thou offer in the morning" [Numbers 28:4]: the singular implies an individual (Menaḥot 65a). The sages said to them: You are not permitted to do so, for a public offering comes only from the property of all Israel; "thou shalt offer" means all Israel, and for that reason it is said in the same section, "shall ye observe to offer unto me" [Numbers 28:2], in the plural. And when they prevailed over them and defeated them, they ordained that they would weigh out their shekels and deposit them in the chamber, and the daily offerings were offered from public funds (Megillat Ta'anit ch. 1). As long as the hand of the Sadducees was uppermost, no doubt the priests acted according to their views; and against them is aimed what the sages said, "You are not permitted to do so," that is, to offer the daily offerings from an individual's donation. And although it is not said explicitly that this happened in Simeon's days, there is no room for doubt about it: the phrase "when they prevailed over them and defeated them" points to a fierce strife and a victory of the Pharisees, and this was in Simeon's days and under the rule of Yannai (Graetz, vol. 3, p. 472). Another ordinance concerning the Temple service, directed against the view of the Sadducees, should also be ascribed to Simeon's time. For the Sadducees said that the red heifer of purification is prepared only by those whose sun has set [after their immersion]; and because of this view the Pharisees ordained that they would actually defile the priest who burns the heifer and then immerse him, so that the heifer would be prepared by a tevul yom (Parah 3:3).⚠1 The account of these things shows that they speak of an incident that actually occurred at some time, when it happened that they prepared a red heifer, and then they enacted this ordinance to make a public demonstration against the Sadducees. The most suitable time for this event and this ordinance was after the victory of the Pharisees, that is, after the death of Yannai, when his son Yoḥanan Hyrcanus was high priest; for at that time they prepared a red heifer. For in the matter of the red heifer it is told that Simeon the Just made two, and Yoḥanan the high priest also made two (ibid. 3:8).⚠2 This is very strange: in the days of Simeon the Just, which were at most forty years (according to the Talmud), they needed two; from then until the days of Yoḥanan the high priest the one that Simeon made sufficed; and in the thirty-one years (or, according to the Talmud, eighty years) that Yoḥanan reigned, one did not suffice them and he had to make two. And it is very unlikely that Yoḥanan made one at his beginning, and afterwards, when he had become a Sadducee and wished to make a demonstration against the Pharisees, made a second by those whose sun had set, according to the view of the Sadducees; for although Yoḥanan followed the Sadducees, it is still not credible that he would cast aspersion on a red heifer that he himself had made. But let us suppose that the tradition of this Mishnah is true in its substance but not exact. It is true that a high priest called Simeon the Just made a red heifer, and it sufficed until the days of the second Simeon the Just, who made another; and from this arose the aggadah that Simeon the Just made two. And so it is with Yoḥanan the high priest: it is true that Yoḥanan the high priest made a red heifer. And indeed in the days of Simeon ben Shetaḥ they strove with all their strength to do things publicly in order to oppose the Sadducees; therefore it is very likely that after Yannai's death, when the hand of the Pharisees grew strong and they enacted many things to subdue the Sadducees, then too they prepared a red heifer by a tevul yom. Both were called by the name of Yoḥanan the high priest because in truth both were made by a high priest named Yoḥanan, except that the first was made by the first Yoḥanan the high priest, the son of Simeon the Hasmonean, and the second was made by Yoḥanan the high priest, the grandson of the first and the son of Yannai. Now we see that in the days of Simeon ben Shetaḥ a red heifer was prepared, and on that occasion they ordained that they would defile the priest who burns the heifer.

1.note: As printed; the defiling and immersing of the priest is in Mishnah Parah 3:7.

2.note: As printed; the list of who made red heifers (Simeon the Just two, Yoḥanan the high priest two) is in Mishnah Parah 3:5.

3.note: The print has no call for this note (the note's number is printed, its call in the text is missing); the call is placed here by the editor, where the note's subject begins.

footnotes.en: See Graetz, vol. 3, p. 516; Sanhedrin (87b and onward), and in the Yerushalmi [Sanhedrin] 11:6. Maimonides, Hilkhot Mamrim ch. 4, followed the Talmud and decided according to R. Meir. In the Yerushalmi this baraita, in which R. Meir, R. Judah and R. Simeon disagree, is not cited; but a view not according to R. Meir is cited in the name of R. Hoshaiah and R. Zeira, and Maimonides paid no attention to this. In our opinion the main view is as we wrote in the text.

The warning "thou shalt not decline from the sentence which they shall shew thee" is said in the section on the rebellious elder. But it is evident that this section was already expounded in early times in two directions. For although it was expounded of the rebellious elder, the plain sense of the verse shows that it speaks of every single person in Israel who rebels against the teaching of the sages and does not act according to their words, and it commands every single one to act "according to the sentence, which they ... shall shew thee" and "according to the sentence of the law which they shall teach thee" [Deuteronomy 17:10–11], and not to decline from the sentence which they shall show. This is the basis for what the later authorities said, that we are commanded concerning all the words of the Scribes by "thou shalt not decline." The proof that the matter was so understood in early times is that they expounded that everything said in the section applies also to the court of Yavneh (Sifre Shofetim §153, and in the Yerushalmi there); and this was not expounded with reference to the rebellious elder, for there is no death penalty for a ruling of the court in Yavneh (Sifre, ibid. §154). This midrash was without doubt expounded immediately after the destruction, when they set up their academy in Yavneh. See part 2, ch. 5, p. 38,⚠1 what I wrote on the first founding of this midrash.

footnotes.en: I will remark here on an aggadah told about Simeon: Once he saw a man running after his fellow into a ruin. Simeon ran after him and saw a sword in his hand, its blood dripping and the slain man writhing. He said to him: Wicked one, who killed this man, I or you? But what can I do, since your blood is not given into my hand, for the Torah said: "At the mouth of two witnesses ... shall he that is worthy of death be put to death" [Deuteronomy 17:6]. So is the reading in Sanhedrin (36b);⚠1 but in the Yerushalmi the reading is: What can I do, since your blood is not given into my hand; but He who knows thoughts will exact punishment, etc. Now in this incident there are two reasons for exemption: first, that Simeon is only one witness; second, that it is testimony by inference (umdana). But from Simeon's words one cannot prove in any way for which reason he said "your blood is not given into my hand": whether because he was only one witness or because his testimony was by inference. Therefore the baraita there, which says, "What is inference? For example, the incident of Simeon ben Shetaḥ," necessarily does not intend to prove that inference is not valid testimony, for this is not proven from the incident. Its intent is only to explain the halakhah in the Mishnah, which says "lest you say [from] inference," that this is not testimony; and this is a settled halakhah and needs no proof. The baraita rather brings an illustration of what testimony by inference is, and says: like the incident of Simeon ben Shetaḥ, where even had there been another witness with Simeon we could not have accepted their testimony. There is no need for the forced explanation of the Tosafists, who wrote that there was another witness with Simeon.

1.note: As printed (the numeral is not fully clear); the story is in Sanhedrin 37b.

footnotes.en: According to the Talmud Simeon was the queen's brother; and by this view we learn further that at that time the halakhah that a sister's husband is disqualified from testifying for him had not yet been introduced (Sanhedrin 27a); for otherwise how could he judge Yannai? Is not one who is disqualified from testifying disqualified from judging (Niddah 49b)?

See the commentary on the Torah by the scholar Knobel, on Exodus 21, who cites there that among the Indian and Greek lawgivers the law of retaliation was literal, not monetary; and according to the testimony of Diodorus, the ancient Egyptians had a statute that plotting witnesses were punished with the same punishment that would have fallen to the accused according to their testimony, and this agrees with the statute of the Torah as the Pharisees understood it. According to the statutes of the Romans in their Twelve Tables, the law of retaliation was literal if the litigants did not wish to settle for money; and later, monetary payment became a fixed statute.

The Pharisees expounded "and they shall spread the cloth": the matters shall be made as clear as a cloth, and it is a figure of speech (Mekhilta, Mishpatim ch. 6 and ch. 13; Sifre Ki Tetze §236; Yerushalmi Ketubbot ch. 4); or they explained: the witnesses of this side and of that side come and make the matter as clear as a cloth, and this too is a figure of speech (Ketubbot 46a; Sifre, ibid.). The words "and spit in his face" they expounded by the rule of likeness and analogy: just as everywhere that the word panim is joined with the letter bet the meaning is not that the act is done on the surface of the face but before the face, as in "stood before you" (amad be-fanekha) and "stand before you" (hityatzev be-fanekha), so in "and spit be-fanav" the meaning is before the face. From this we learn that they sometimes expounded the words of the Torah figuratively; and we learn further that they interpreted by the rule of likeness and analogy, and this is the basis of the gezerah shavah, which is one of the hermeneutical rules (middot).
